title: Learning prejudice: Lloyd Reese and a junior-college friend
summary: Lloyd Reese tells him not to use a racial slur, and a wrestling incident with a Black classmate shows him how words hurt.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So I do know a little bit about prejudice but I know

I myself used the word "nigger," not knowing that was a bad term until years later. I had a friend, Lloyd Reese, and one day he said, "You know, Jim, I know how you think, but please don't use that word anymore." I said, "What's wrong with it?" He said, "That's not a good word." I said, "What do you mean it's not a good word? What should I say?" He said, "Well, call us Negroes or even call us Oxford Grays, but don't call us niggers." And I wanted to die, you know. I sank into the ground. So then I spent the next month thinking how many times I'd used that word to the wrong people.

In junior college I had this black guy I used to wrestle with and box. And I did know about prejudice because I was a little surprised at junior college, he was sort of in with this bunch of guys, musicians and sort of like a hep crowd there that I was with, being a musician. And we would all go to the dances together and I remember we would dance with his girlfriend and he would dance with white girls and I do remember I was surprised. So I did know a little about prejudice.

And I also remember, once we were wrestling or something and he hurt me and I called him a black bastard. Now, when I said a black bastard, it didn't mean race. Like they say a black Irishman, that's an Irishman that's lost his faith. And a black bastard was another guy that was a dirty bastard. It had nothing to do with his race but as I saw this look in

his eyes it dawned on me, this guy is black. And I thought he was going to kill me. I didn't know whether I was frightened or heartbroken. I started to cry and apologize because I knew I'd hurt his feelings.
